You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure of this public goods game: keeping a token in my own account gives me +1 but costs each of the other three members -0.3, while putting it in the group account only gives me +0.3 with no direct effect on others, so I need to think about how self-interest versus collective benefit plays out here.

Comparing totals, keeping all tokens yields a net social surplus per token of 1 - 0.9 = 0.1, while contributing yields 0.3, so cooperation is better for the group as a whole, but keeping is still individually dominant since 1 > 0.3 regardless of what others do. That means the Nash equilibrium is everyone keeping all 20 tokens and contributing zero to the group, even though mutual cooperation would leave everyone better off — I'm now comparing the full outcomes under each scenario to see the gap between individual and collective rationality.
